title: Twelve months close
hook: two poets, twelve months each, one longing

segments.voice: Yesterday, winter's union, and your line was he comes home. Did you pause on your own threshold and notice you were home? Today Guru Nanak's year comes to its end. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-eight.

Two and ten. That's how the last stanza of Guru Nanak's poem counts the months: not twelve, but be das, two and ten, the way someone might count on their fingers at the end of a long year. Once the Beloved has come home, the poem looks back over the whole of it. And the Guru Granth Sahib holds a second year just like it, by Guru Arjan, in Raga Majh. Two poets, twelve months each. Today, before we leave the calendar behind: what the two years share, and what a year of longing leaves behind. Twelve months close.
screen: `TWO AND TEN.` → `NANAK LOOKS BACK OVER THE YEAR.` → `A SECOND YEAR, BY GURU ARJAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the end of Nanak's year, given in plain English, not word for word. The two and ten months, the seasons, the dates, the days are good. The hours, the moments, the instants are blessed, when the True One comes and the meeting happens with ease. Hold that beside everything this week has walked through. Spring was good, and she ached. The hot months were good, and she burned. The rains were good, and she lay awake. Nothing about the weather was wrong. What changed was the meeting, and once it came, every month looked different looking back. Even the hard ones. Now set Guru Arjan's year beside it, which this path read in year two. His months are in Raga Majh, and they too move from Chet around to Phalgun. They too belong to a bride, separated and asking to be united. In his Chet, remembering the Lord brings joy. In his Asarh, the heat burns the ones who don't keep the Lord near. Two Gurus, two ragas, two voices, and they share the bones: a calendar the farmer and the bride both know, a longing in every month, and an ending where the time itself is blessed. That's what a Barah Maha does. It doesn't wait for one perfect season. It takes the ordinary year, every page of it, and lets each month carry the same love. So the close of these days is simple. Not one season is left out. That's today's line: every season longs.
screen: `TWO AND TEN MONTHS ARE GOOD.` · `THE MEETING CHANGES THE YEAR.` · `GURU ARJAN'S YEAR, IN MAJH.` · `SAME BONES: A YEAR OF LONGING.` · then, large: `EVERY SEASON LONGS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: compare two seasons you've known. Sit, and let your breath slow. Bring back one season of your life that felt like waiting: a hard winter, a long hot stretch, a time when someone or something was missing. Let a few details come back, the light, the smell, where you lived. Then bring back a season that felt like arriving. Hold the two side by side. Notice what's the same in both, the part of you that was longing all along. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath, thanking God for both seasons. The bell holds the time.
Twelve months close. Guru Nanak's year ends by calling every month, day and moment good once the True One comes, and Guru Arjan's year in Majh shares the same longing. Today's word.
Your line: every season longs. Today, name the season you're in, outside and inside, and say one good thing about it, even if it's a waiting one. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Both Barah Mahas are sung in kirtan and read in the Guru Granth Sahib; in some gurdwaras Guru Arjan's stanza for the new month is read on Sangrand, the first day of the month.
